nameStory: Castor-aralia gets its name from its large, palm-shaped leaves that look remarkably similar to those of the castor bean plant (though they're not related at all!). The 'aralia' part connects it to its botanical family, which includes other plants with similar leaf arrangements. It's also called 'prickly castor oil tree' because of the sharp spines that cover its trunk and branches.
description: Castor-aralia is a striking deciduous tree that can grow 40-60 feet tall with a distinctive tropical appearance despite being cold-hardy. Its most eye-catching feature is its enormous, deeply-lobed leaves that can span over a foot across, resembling giant hands with 5-9 finger-like segments. The trunk and branches are armored with fierce-looking spines, making this tree both beautiful and formidable. Originally from northeastern Asia, it's planted as an ornamental in New England gardens and parks.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Massive, palm-shaped leaves up to 16 inches across with 5-9 deep lobes that feel smooth and somewhat thick to the touch. They're arranged alternately on branches and have long, sturdy petioles (leaf stems).

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Trunk and younger branches are densely covered with sharp, cone-shaped spines that can be over an inch long. The bark beneath is gray-brown with a relatively smooth texture between the spines.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, creamy-white flowers appear in late summer in large, umbrella-like clusters at branch tips. Each tiny flower has 5 petals and gives off a faintly sweet fragrance.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small, round, blue-black berries about 1/4 inch across that ripen in fall. They're arranged in the same umbrella-shaped clusters as the flowers and feel slightly waxy.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a single-trunked tree with a relatively open, irregular crown. Branches tend to be thick and somewhat horizontal, giving it an exotic, architectural appearance.

habitat: In New England, castor-aralia is found almost exclusively as a planted ornamental tree in gardens, parks, and arboretums rather than growing wild. It prefers well-drained, fertile soil and can tolerate both full sun and partial shade. You're most likely to encounter it at botanical gardens, college campuses, or in the yards of adventurous gardeners who appreciate unusual trees.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge relatively late in spring, unfolding from large, pointed buds. The massive leaves are initially bronze-tinted before turning bright green.
seasonality.summer: The huge, tropical-looking leaves are at their most impressive, creating dense shade. Late summer brings the creamy-white flower clusters that attract various pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn a lovely clear yellow before dropping, while the blue-black berries ripen and may persist after leaf fall. The spiny architecture becomes more visible.
seasonality.winter: The distinctive spiny trunk and branches are fully exposed, making identification easy even from a distance. Large, pointed buds are visible at branch tips.

funFact: Despite looking like it belongs in a tropical rainforest, castor-aralia can survive temperatures down to -20°F and is actually more cold-hardy than many native New England trees, thanks to its origins in the harsh winters of northern Asia!
confusionNotes: The huge, lobed leaves might remind you of a maple, but no maple has leaves nearly this large or has spines on its trunk. The spiny bark makes it unmistakable once you see it - no other tree in New England has such impressive armor.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - despite being called 'prickly castor oil tree,' this plant is completely unrelated to the castor bean plant that produces castor oil. It's also sometimes called 'tree aralia' to distinguish it from smaller shrubby aralias, though it's the only tree-sized member of this family you'll encounter in New England.
compareHints: Castor-aralia is the only species in its genus Kalopanax, making it truly one-of-a-kind. Within the aralia family, it's easily distinguished from other members by its tree size and spiny trunk - other aralias in New England are typically shrubs or small plants without the dramatic spines. The combination of massive palmate leaves and a spiny trunk is unique among all trees in our region.
